extracted.intended_audience: federal agencies and agency rulemaking officials (e.g., rulewriters, docket managers, e-Rulemaking staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Official recommendations and best practices for how federal agencies should design, manage, and evaluate notice-and-comment (including e‑Rulemaking) processes, public comment handling, dockets, administrative records, and use of social media and websites to promote participation and preserve records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comment‑analysis software
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider using reliable comment analysis software to organize and review public comments, especially when comment volume is large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5 U.S.C. § 553 requires agencies to consider all comments received, but does not require that a person read every identical or nearly identical comment; agencies should share experiences and best practices with the eRulemaking PMO and interagency counterparts when using such software.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process for flagging inappropriate or protected content
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should explore providing a method (including for members of the public) for flagging inappropriate or protected content in submitted comments and for taking appropriate action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with the eRulemaking PMO and interagency counterparts to develop flagging mechanisms and follow-up procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism to identify confidential/trade_secret submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should explore mechanisms that allow a commenter to indicate prior to or upon submittal that a comment contains confidential or trade secret information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear avenues for marking confidentiality at submission time to enable appropriate handling under applicable law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures to review and handle confidential information
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should confirm they have procedures in place to review comments identified as containing confidential or trade secret information and determine how such information should be handled in accordance with law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish and document internal review workflows and legal compliance processes for handling assertedly confidential materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess Privacy Act compliance (FDMS SORN)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should assess whether the FDMS System of Records Notice provides sufficient Privacy Act compliance for their uses of Regulations.gov and consider changes if warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with the eRulemaking PMO to evaluate privacy protections and update SORN language or practices when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic records in lieu of paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may use electronic records instead of paper records for rulemaking dockets, consistent with the APA and NARA determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine agency records schedules to determine when destruction of paper copies scanned into an approved electronic recordkeeping system is permitted; follow schedule and NARA requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include supporting studies/reports in electronic docket
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should include in the publicly available electronic docket all studies and reports on which the proposal for rulemaking draws, as soon as practicable, except to the extent they are protected from disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post relevant scientific and technical findings timely (see Exec. Order 13,563 §2(b)); do not withhold documents absent appropriate FOIA/exemption justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive entries for physical objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should include in the electronic docket a descriptive entry or photograph for all physical objects received during the comment period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comments include non-electronic materials, create accessible descriptive metadata or images so the public and reviewers can understand content without physical access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide electronic records to courts
rubrics_metrics.description: In litigation, agencies should work early with parties and courts to provide electronic copies of the rulemaking record in lieu of paper, particularly for large records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should embrace electronic filing and minimize paper requirements; the Judicial Conference should consider facilitating electronic-review practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record schedules must include e‑Rulemaking records
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies, when implementing Federal Records Act responsibilities, should ensure their records schedules include records generated during e‑Rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update schedules to account for email, web content, social media records, and other electronic artifacts created during rule development and commenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish guidance on effective comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The eRulemaking PMO should publish a document explaining what types of comments are most beneficial and listing best practices for parties submitting comments; agencies may publish supplements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make these documents publicly available (agency website, Regulations.gov) to promote widespread availability; include examples, templates, or webinars to illustrate high‑quality comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set appropriate comment period lengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should set comment periods that balance public participation and efficient rulemaking; generally use at least 60 days for significant regulatory actions and at least 30 days for other rulemakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When setting shorter periods, provide an explanation; consider the nature of the rule, complexity, and stakeholder needs when choosing duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely posting of public comments online
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should adopt stated policies to post public comments to the Internet within a specified period after submission, including posting electronically submitted comments and scanning/posting paper comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post comments on Regulations.gov or agency dockets in a timely manner regardless of submission method; adopt and publish timeframes for posting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish and clarify anonymous comment policies
rubrics_metrics.description: The eRulemaking PMO and individual agencies should establish and publish policies regarding the submission and treatment of anonymous comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make policies visible and accessible on agency websites and in docket materials so commenters understand the consequences and procedures for anonymity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Late comment policies and consistent application
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should adopt and publish policies on late comments, apply them consistently within each rulemaking, and announce the policy in public forums and Federal Register notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether late submissions will be accepted, whether they are disfavored, and that they will be considered to the extent practicable; apply uniformly within a rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reply comment periods / further input opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriate, agencies should make use of reply comment periods or other opportunities for public input on submitted comments after posting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reply opportunities can be written reply periods, oral hearings, or other means; consider supplemental notice when comments or agency responses present new or important issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring staleness of comments and refreshing the record
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should not automatically deem comments stale after a fixed time but should monitor dockets and, where circumstances have materially changed, consider supplemental notices or other mechanisms to refresh the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether factual or legal changes warrant reopening comment or issuing an additional NPRM to ensure the record supports final action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design websites with rulemaking participation in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should design and manage their web presence (including mobile) to promote public participation in rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid burying rulemaking information; consider 'top tasks' but ensure rulemaking remains discoverable and accessible even if not high-traffic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a one‑stop location for pending rulemakings
rubrics_metrics.description: Each agency should provide access to an easily reachable one‑stop location from its home page listing all pending rulemakings and highlighting those open for comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use links to centralized resources (Regulations.gov, RegInfo.gov, Federal Register 2.0) or agency-maintained lists that extract centralized data to keep information current without duplicative database maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make comment policies easy to locate
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should display or link to their comment policies in prominent or multiple locations on their websites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure comment-submission instructions, anonymity policies, moderation rules, and late-submission policies are visible where users submit or view comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve website accessibility and inclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should improve website accessibility and take steps to increase participation by those who have faced barriers (non‑English speakers, low‑bandwidth users, individuals with disabilities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide multilingual outlets where appropriate, low‑bandwidth options, accessible design conforming to applicable standards, and outreach tailored to underrepresented stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and make retrievable materials from completed rulemakings
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should develop systematic protocols to enable online storage and retrieval of materials from completed rulemakings and ensure old URLs redirect to current locations where feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create archival practices and web redirects so historical materials remain discoverable for legal, historical, and public-use purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic evaluation and innovation in internet use
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should periodically evaluate their use of the Internet in rulemaking and continue to innovate and experiment with cost‑effective ways to engage the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct usability testing, measure outreach effectiveness, pilot new tools, and collaborate interagency to identify best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage centralized data sources to improve info availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should leverage centralized data sources (e.g., Regulations.gov) to improve the availability of rulemaking information on agency sites without maintaining duplicate databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use APIs or data feeds where possible to surface up‑to‑date rulemaking information with minimal cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore use of social media for outreach and consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should explore social media and web-based interactive technologies to provide opportunities for public consultation, discussion, and engagement, particularly for outreach, education, and reaching underrepresented stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social media to raise awareness, inform about how to comment, and to solicit dispersed knowledge; clearly explain how any social-media interaction will be used and integrate it thoughtfully into the rulemaking process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set clear goals before using social media in notice‑and‑comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Before using social media in connection with a particular rulemaking, agencies should identify specific goals they expect to achieve and carefully consider costs and benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select tools that fit the goals and integrate them into the traditional rulemaking process; do not presume social media always produces high-quality input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose how sponsored social media discussions will be treated
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency sponsors a social-media discussion, it should prominently indicate to the public whether and how the discussion will be treated under the APA and the rulemaking record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include: (a) include all agency‑administered social media comments in the record (consider API/technological transfer); or (b) state that the discussion will not be included and provide clear instructions for submitting official comments; use conspicuous disclaimers on the social media site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a user‑friendly NPRM version for social media input
rubrics_metrics.description: When soliciting input through social media, agencies should provide a 'friendly' and clear version of the NPRM for lay users (summaries, hyperlinked definitions, layered content).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either publish both versions in the Federal Register or cross-reference the user-friendly and official versions so participants can find both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use facilitators for social media discussions when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider retaining facilitator services to manage rulemaking discussions via social media when participants are inexperienced or issues are highly divisive/emotional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitators can encourage substantive, reasoned comments, ask follow-ups, and foster productive dialogue; consider facilitators for targeted engagement of novice commenters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming crowdsourcing benefits all rulemakings
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should recognize that not all rulemakings will be enhanced by crowdsourcing; use public submission when the public's response is itself the subject (e.g., format testing) or when lay situated knowledge is valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design outreach to solicit substantive individualized comments from organizations' members rather than mass, undifferentiated reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider collaborative drafting and ranking tools carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider experimenting with collaborative drafting platforms and, if using ranking/voting tools, explain how the input will be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about the purpose and limits of crowd input and how it informs agency decisions; avoid creating impressions that rulemaking is a plebiscite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use social media for notification of final actions and compliance info
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should use social media to notify and educate the public about final agency actions produced through rulemaking and, where appropriate, to provide compliance information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social media to disseminate practical guidance (e.g., paperwork requirements) and to reach affected audiences post‑promulgation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate interagency on social media best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should collaborate to identify and share best practices addressing issues that arise in the use of social media in rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interagency sharing can produce standardized guidance, educational materials, and platform usage protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use social media to test for objections before direct final rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider using social media before or in connection with direct final rulemaking to quickly identify significant or meaningful objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, early engagement via social channels can surface objections that would preclude direct final approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider First Amendment and moderation policies for social media
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider how the First Amendment applies to facilitating or hosting social-media discussions and post a comment policy that indicates moderation will be viewpoint‑neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may define or restrict topics, impose reasonable decorum rules, prevent spam, and explain moderation policies clearly to participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure ex parte and PRA policies address social media
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies with ex parte contact policies should review them to ensure they address communications made through social media; consider Paperwork Reduction Act implications of social media inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update policies to cover new communication channels and consult OMB guidance on social media and PRA compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'rulemaking record' and 'considered' materials for administrative record
rubrics_metrics.description: The rulemaking record should mean the full record of materials before the agency in an informal rulemaking and include materials that were 'considered'—reviewed by an individual with substantive responsibilities with some minimum degree of attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A document is 'considered' if reviewed to evaluate its possible significance unless the review shows it is not germane; do not exclude documents merely because the agency disagrees with them or will not rely on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public rulemaking docket = public version of record; maximize disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The public rulemaking docket is the public version of the rulemaking record (online or physical) including all information the agency has made available for public viewing; agencies should manage dockets to achieve maximum disclosure consistent with prudential limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish internal records from public dockets and be transparent about redactions or withheld materials consistent with legal exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop agency guidance on compilation/preservation/certification of records
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should develop and publish guidance to aid personnel compiling rulemaking and administrative records and to increase public understanding of agency recordkeeping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance should describe processes for compiling the administrative record, certifying completeness, preserving electronic artifacts, and documenting retention/schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage transition from paper to electronic records in accord with NARA/OMB
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should design IT and recordkeeping resources mindful of principles and best practices to facilitate electronic recordkeeping, preservation, and access as they transition from paper to electronic formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow OMB/NARA directives (e.g., managing government records directives and deadlines) and ensure permanent electronic records are handled appropriately.
